data.narrative: Student diagnosed two race conditions in URL shortener redirect handler: (1) duplicate-key on concurrent INSERT fixed with atomic upsert ON CONFLICT, (2) lost-update on timestamp under concurrent writes fixed by consolidating INSERT + UPDATE into single atomic operation using database now(). Student chose synthetic reproduction over production replay, creating minimal 10-concurrent-request script that deterministically triggers both bugs.

dimension_scores.observation: Student formed specific testable hypotheses: identified concurrency on popular links as root cause variable, distinguished check-then-act and lost-update as two distinct race mechanisms.
dimension_scores.evidence: Student stated: concurrency was actual variable because reproduction script isolates it directly; same endpoint, code, data, only thing changed is 10 simultaneous requests vs sequential.

dimension_scores.observation: Student understood need to compare log timestamps against database values to detect silent corruption but did not actively parse structured log output during diagnosis.
dimension_scores.evidence: Student recognized: redirect count looks correct but last_accessed_at might not match last request timestamp. Awareness of log-to-database comparison but execution deferred.

dimension_scores.observation: Student communicated findings clearly throughout module, distinguished two separate race conditions, explained danger of each, articulated decision rationale tied to observed symptoms.

dimension_scores.observation: Student understood underlying mechanisms not just symptoms: check-then-act atomicity gap, lost-update race on concurrent writes, why database now() vs Python datetime.now() matters.
dimension_scores.evidence: Student articulated: the one completing last overwrites with earlier timestamp. Proposed server-side now(): single atomic operation ensures no Python-to-database timing window.

strengths: Strong hypothesis formation: identified concurrency as key variable before testing, used synthetic reproduction to isolate deterministically.
Deep pattern recognition: understood check-then-act vs lost-update as distinct patterns, identified where pattern exists in codebase.
Silent corruption awareness: recognized silent data corruption more dangerous than loud errors, directly connected fix to business risk.
Atomic operation reasoning: correctly identified database now() superior to Python datetime.now() under concurrency.
data.recommendation: In Module 4 (Performance Debugging), apply same variable-isolation approach: form hypothesis about what is slow, create minimal test measuring suspected bottleneck, use profiling/tracing to confirm. Reproduction skill transfers directly to performance diagnosis.

public_evidence.student_action: Diagnosed and fixed two race conditions: check-then-act duplicate-key race on INSERT, lost-update race on timestamp field.
public_evidence.technical_detail: Changed from separate INSERT then UPDATE to atomic INSERT...ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE using database now().
public_evidence.proof: INSERT INTO click_events (link_id, clicked_at, last_accessed_at) VALUES (:link_id, now(), now()) ON CONFLICT (link_id) DO UPDATE SET last_accessed_at = now()
public_evidence.ability: Identifies race conditions in concurrent database writes and implements atomic fixes using SQL patterns.
public_evidence.reviewer_value: Shows understanding of concurrency pitfalls, check-then-act and lost-update races, SQL atomicity guarantees.

concepts_demonstrated.evidence: Identified pattern: SELECT followed by separate INSERT/UPDATE without atomicity. Fixed via ON CONFLICT.
Explained: concurrent requests update same row, one completing last overwrites with earlier timestamp. Fixed via atomic upsert.
Distinguished: sequential requests would fail if data/timing issue; they don't — concurrency is root cause.
Chose synthetic: form testable hypothesis, run cheapest thing proving/disproving it.
Recognized database now() eliminates Python-to-database timing window through atomic operation.

teaching_approaches.detail: Module provided concrete 500-error symptom on popular links leading to hypothesis that concurrency was variable. Student created 10-concurrent-request reproduction confirming deterministically.
Module described silent timestamp corruption (no errors but wrong data), forcing look beyond error logs and inspect database field values.

Able to reason about mechanisms when guided to look at data
